title: The field of Siffin
hook: Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's meet, Qur'ans are raised on spears, and arbitration is agreed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Battle of the Camel, Ammar, and a verse about two parties of believers. Your line was believers against believers. Did you honor someone you disagree with? Day eight hundred eighty-three.

Spears go up along a battle line, and on their points are not banners but pages. Pages of the Qur'an. The army holding them is Syrian, led by Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria and a kinsman of Uthman. The army facing them is Ali's. They have fought for days on a plain near the Euphrates, and the histories say Ali's side was pressing hard. Then the pages rise, and a call goes across the field: let the Book of God judge between us. Every soldier on Ali's side now has to decide what those pages mean. Today, the place where this happened.
screen: `SPEARS GO UP.` → `PAGES, NOT BANNERS.` → `LET THE BOOK JUDGE.`

segments.voice: Mu'awiyah had refused to pledge to Ali until Uthman's killers were handed over. Ali held that Mu'awiyah must first accept his caliphate. Neither would move, and the armies met at Siffin. The raised pages, the histories say, were the idea of Amr ibn al-As, on Mu'awiyah's side. Was it a sincere call to the Qur'an, or a way to stop a losing fight? The sources leave room for both readings. Ali, reports say, suspected a stratagem. But soldiers in his own ranks would not fight against the raised pages, and they pressed him to accept. He agreed to arbitration: one man chosen by each side, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali, Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiyah, to judge by the Qur'an and the Prophet's way. Bukhari preserves a voice from those days. Sahl ibn Hunayf, who was with Ali, tells his own side: suspect your own opinion. He reminds them of Hudaybiyyah, years before, when the Prophet accepted a truce that looked like a defeat, and Umar had objected, and the truce turned out to be an opening. The point he draws for them: a settlement can be right even when it feels like losing. How Muslims judge Siffin differs. In Sunni teaching, Ali was in the right and Mu'awiyah erred in his judgment, while Mu'awiyah is still counted a companion. Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam and read the pages as a trick. Either way, the picture stays: pages on the spears, and a battle stopped for words.
screen: `NEITHER WOULD MOVE.` · `AMR'S IDEA, THE HISTORIES SAY.` · `ONE JUDGE FROM EACH SIDE.` · `SUSPECT YOUR OWN OPINION.` · then, large: `PAGES ON THE SPEARS.`

segments.voice: The practice: agree to talk. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a standoff you're part of, where neither side will move first. Breathe in, and notice the voice that says talking now would be losing. Breathe out, and borrow Sahl's words for a moment: suspect your own opinion. Not drop it. Just hold it a little more loosely. Then think of one small offer to talk you could make, a message, a time, a neutral place. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart in it. The bell holds the time.
Siffin, the plain near the Euphrates: where Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's met, pages of the Qur'an were raised on spears, and arbitration was agreed. Today's word.

Your line: pages on the spears. Today, when someone quotes a rule or a text at you mid-argument, ask yourself honestly whether it's a call to agree or a way to win, and then whether the same is true of you. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims study Siffin as part of the history of the fitnah; Sunni teaching holds Ali was in the right while counting Mu'awiyah a companion, and Shia Muslims regard Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam.

trapdoor: what you thought: Siffin was just another battle.
what it means: a battle stopped when pages of the Qur'an were raised on spears, and arbitration agreed.
what a scholar hears: Sahl ibn Hunayf's words in Bukhari, the choice of Abu Musa and Amr as judges, and the arbitration that would split Ali's own army.
